newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank to approve gold plan - Bonn sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank to approve gold plan - Bonn sources.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank on Wednesday is expected to approve a revaluation of its gold reserves that could swell German federal finances by up to 12 billion marks ($7.1 billion) in 1997, government sources said on Tuesday.

The gold revaluation plan is part of proposals by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue central bank reserves in a bid to help Germany's 1997 budget, straining to meet Maastricht criteria for European monetary union.

Waigel himself told journalists in Frankfurt on Tuesday that a special interim Bundesbank balance sheet had been drawn up and that as a result Bonn could receive a payout from such reserve revaluations this year.

Government sources said the central bank, whose council is holding a regular meeting on Wednesday, would issue a statement outlining its position on a planned revaluation of its gold reserves. This week's meeting is being held on Wednesday, one day earlier than usual, as Thursday is a public holiday.

They said the Bundesbank had in principle accepted the plan, announced by Waigel amid great controversy two weeks ago, and that the finance ministry had already informed it of the required changes to the bank's constitution.
Neither Finance Minister Theo Waigel nor his State Secretary Juergen Stark would as a result need to attend the council meeting, the sources added.
Waigel, in Frankfurt to attend a commemoration of the Marshall Plan, told journalists on the fringe of the ceremony that other technical details had already been sorted out.

"An interim balance sheet has been drawn up and a payout is possible in 1997, Waigel said. Usually, Bonn gets a yearly payout of Bundesbank profits every April and has thus already received its portion for 1996.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in reserve valued at well below current market levels.
Coalition sources said a revaluation towards market prices could boost federal finances by an extra 10 billion to 12 billion marks in 1997 and by a similar amount in 1998.
Any such revenues would be a possible lifeline to Waigel following the unveiling of an estimated 18 billion mark shortfall in 1997 tax revenues earlier this month.

Confusion remains however on whether Bonn can in fact use the measure to cut back its 1997 budget deficit to the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) required for entry into the single European currency.
Waigel has defended the plan as a necessary reform of Bundesbank accounting procedures ahead of EMU and has insisted there are no plans to sell any of the central bank's gold.

The revaluation plan is one of a number of possible budgetary moves Germany has recently announced it is planning ahead of currency union and which have led to howls of protest that it is cooking its books.

Earlier, coalition sources said the government was now considering selling 287 million shares in phone company Deutsche Telekom AG this year and offloading its remaining stake by the end of 1998 for budgetary purposes.
